Burnet County Commissioners Court’s                                                 2
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
           Burnet County Commissioners Court (“BCCC”) respectfully addresses the

Exceptions to Proposal for Decision (Exceptions) filed by Oncor and other intervenors in

this case and Requests that the Commission accept the Findings of Fact and Conclusions

of Laws as set forth in the PFD, with one exception as to BCCC’s emergency management

communication systems.

    I.       SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

          BCCC continues to agree with the PFD that Oncor Electric Delivery Company

LLC. (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation (“LCRA”) (together

“Applicants”) failed to meet their burdens in their Joint Application and that the Joint

Application should be denied.

          BCCC also continues to agree with the PFD that Applicants failed to provide

landowners with proper notice under the Commission’s rules.

          Finally, Applicants did not carry their burden to show need for these massive

745kV transmission lines at this time.

          Alternatively, if the Commission decides to grant the Applicants’ Joint Application,

BCCC requests that the Commission add ordering paragraphs providing necessary

protections against interference by transmission towers and lines with Burnet County’s

emergency management communication systems and its connection to the Statewide

Interoperability Communication System.

    II.      NOTICE

          BCCC agrees that Applicants did not provide notice of the Joint Application in

accordance with 16 TAC §22.52 (3) and (4). Applicants argue that “[t]he plain language

of the 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) §22.52(a), Commission precedent and



Burnet County Commissioners Court’s            3
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
 practical consideration all compel conclusions that are contrary” to the PFD. However, the

Commission need not consider anything beyond the plain language of the rules.1 The

argument centers on the word “current.”

        A.        Current Tax Rolls

        The ALJs noted that several intervenors challenge whether Applicants satisfied the

requirement that notice was mailed to landowners “as stated on the current county tax

rolls.2 The ALJs provided detailed analysis of the data Applicants used and considered the

record evidence provided by the Applicants and the intervenors.3 Applicants stated that

they served notice to all landowners “at the time they pulled the data from the county tax

rolls.”4 The record evidence shows that the Applicants pulled data for the Environmental

Assessment (EA) between December 2024 and March 2026.5 Furthermore, the record

evidence shows that the tracts reflected on the Applicants’ interactive map were identified

between May 2025 and February 2026.6

        Intervenors presented discovery responses from Applicants, their own testimony

and records, and records from county tax appraisal districts. Over three dozen directly

affected landowners did not receive timely notice of the Application. 7 The ALJs

determined that Applicants did not use “current” information.




        1
            City of San Antonio v. Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., 506 S.W.3d 630 (Tex App. 2016).
        2 PFD at 28-37; 16 TAC 22.52(a)(3).

        3 Id.

        4 TR. Vol 3 at 19:2-5 (June 10, 2026).

        5 BCCC Ex. 5 (Applicants’ Resp. to BCCC’s Second RFIs) at BCCC000100.

        6 Id. at BCCC000099.

        7 PFD at 36; App. Ex. 7 at 7-10; App. Ex. 19 at 2; JKK Panel Ex. 10 at 28-29); Tr. Vol. 3 at 12:1-

16:14; 16:2-17:22; and 18:2-19:6 (June 10, 2026).


Burnet County Commissioners Court’s                 4
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
          Applicants assert that “current county tax rolls” is undefined.8 The term does not

need a definition. The plain language of the rule suffices. “Current” is defined by Merriam-

Webster Dictionary as an adjective meaning “occurring in or existing at the present time.”
9
    Instead, Applicants change the definition of “current” to mean “the most recently

available data in a manner that can be sorted, verified, and prepared in time to mail

thousands of notices on the same date the application is filed.”10 There is nothing in the

record evidence or in Commission precedence to support Applicants’ definition.

         Applicants then point to Project No. 58400 in support of their position. Applicants

quote the Commission’s response to the Office of Public Utility Counsel’s (“OPUC”)

suggestion that the rule be amended to track the Water Code.11 However, that response

must be considered in the context of OPUC’s recommendations. The Commission rejected

OPUC’s proposed modification, stating that the modification was unnecessary because the

rule entitles directly affected landowners to notice. Applicants’ interpretation of the

Commission’s intent would mean the directly affected landowners at the time the

application is filed would not need to receive notice. Another interpretation of the

Commission’s comment could effectively require Applicants to identify and notify all

directly affected landowners, even if the tax rolls were inaccurate as of the date the

Application was filed. The latter interpretation is more in line with what due process really

requires. Applicants read far more into the Commission’s simple decision to leave the rule

unchanged than the text or context of that decision supports.


         8   Applicants’ Exceptions to Proposal for Decision (Applicants’ Exceptions) at. p. 54 (Sept. 2,
2026).
         9 https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/current.

         10 Applicants’ Exceptions at 55.

         11 Id. at 56.



Burnet County Commissioners Court’s                 5
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
         Applicants’ failure to provide proper notice does not end there. The Applicants’

Environmental Analysis (“EA”) is inherently tied to the data Applicants relied upon when

the EA was prepared. When intervenors presented Applicants with verifiable information

demonstrating that the EA’s data were inaccurate or outdated, Applicants nevertheless

refused to update the EA.

        The EA is intended to identify habitable structures and other relevant information

that informs the routing analysis. Because Applicants refused to incorporate verified,

current information into the EA, the information underlying the routing analysis was stale

and, therefore, unreliable. Applicants cannot reasonably rely on an EA that they knew

contained outdated information while simultaneously using that information to support

their routing and notice determinations.

        B.        Public Meeting Notice

        In general, administrative rules, which have the same force as statutes, are

construed in the same manner as statutes.12 An agency must follow the clear, unambiguous

language of its own rules.13 The language of the Commission’s Rule 22.52(a) is clear and

unambiguous. Applicants did not comply with the rule because they did not provide direct

mail notice of at least one public meeting to each of the persons listed on the current county

tax rolls as an owner of land within 500 feet of the centerline.14 To read the rule any other

way would be to ignore the plain language of the rule.




        12
           Centerpoint Energy Houston Elec., LLC v. Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., 408 SW3d 910, 916 (Tex.
App. 2013).
        13
             Id. at 916-917; Rodriguez v. Service Lloyds Ins. Co., 070199, 977 S.W.2d 248, 254 (Tex. 1999).
        14
             16 TAC 25.52(a)(4).


Burnet County Commissioners Court’s                  6
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
         Applicants point to several cases to cite precedent for its position. Applicants also,

cite to Docket No. 59315, 15 a docket in which there is still time for file a motion for

rehearing and appeal.16

        Applicants cited to Docket No. 1101417 in their Reply Brief.18 The Administrative

Law Judges (ALJs) reviewed Docket No. 11014 and found that the case was not helpful

because at the time, the Commission’s rules did not require open houses (public

meetings).19 Open houses were used to show the level of community input.20 The case

can further be distinguished by the size of the line, the number of intervenors and the

willingness of the transmission provider to abate the case multiple times, and the

continuation of active negotiations with the landowners.21

        Applicants then cite Docket No. 45624 stating that the City of Garland’s (Garland)

two public meetings were sufficient even though Garland modified and added new

segments in response to feedback without holding additional public meetings.22 This case

is not in any way comparable because as stated in the SOAH PFD, notice was not a

 contested issue and the intervenors remaining at the time of the hearing filed a joint

stipulation!23

        Next Applicants cite Docket No. 49523, which again is distinguishable from the

facts in this case.24 In Docket 49523, the intervenor complaining of lack of notice did not

get notice because they were not a directly affected landowner at any point in the

proceeding.25 The landowner who agreed to take the line was next to the complaining

intervenor. 26 Per the Commission’s rules, only those who are directly affected by the

modification must receive notice. 27 ALJ Linda Brite was one of the ALJ’s in Docket

49523.28 She must have also seen the distinction because she was a presiding ALJ in this

case and decided differently, when approximately 1400 additional directly-affected

landowners were added after the public meetings.29

        Finally, Applicants cite Docket No. 51023 as support that notice was sufficient with

the original public meetings.30 However, no party challenged the sufficiency of notice or

Burnet County Commissioners Court’s                  8
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
 asserted that a directly affected landowner had not been property noticed. 31 Rather, a

landowner contended that it should have received notice even though it was not a directly

affected landowner. The landowner was adjacent to, not crossed by, the proposed

transmission line.32 Further, there were no habitable structures on his property within 300

feet of the centerline.33

           The cases cited by Applicants in support of their exceptions are of little use to the

case at hand, as described above. Also of note is that the cases to which Applicants cited

were all under a one-year schedule but often took longer. And none of them had the volume

of intervenors or the length and size of the line as is in this case.

           The PFD’s analysis of notice was correct and should be adopted by the

Commission. These notice issues raise serious due process concerns.

    III.        ADDITIONAL DUE PROCESS ISSUES

           BCCC agrees with Brady Creek Intervenors and Solana Intervenors that the

 compressed schedule for the hearing on the merits caused great prejudice to the parties.34

 Intervenors were not aware until the first day of the hearing that they would be allocated

 a mere 13 minutes each to cross-examine the Applicants’ panel of eight witnesses. There

 was not sufficient time to examine any issues sufficiently. Further, with the Applicants’

 insistence on a 10 business-day response deadline for discovery propounded onto them,

 the answers would not be due until mid-hearing. Additionally, Intervenors were only

  allowed seven minutes for the PUCT Staff witness and three minutes to cross intervenor

 witnesses.

          In conjunction with the notice issues and overall condensed time-schedule with the

 record numbers of intervenors, landowners due process rights were violated.

    IV.        CONSTRAINTS

          No party made exceptions to the PFD relating to BCCC Emergency Management

Communications towers. Therefore, BCCC relies on its Exceptions to the PFD. BCCC

includes in this Reply to Exceptions proposed findings of fact and conclusions law, infra.

    V.         NEED

          As the ALJ’s found in the PFD, the circumstances have changed since the Permian

 Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) was first approved by the Commission in 2024.35 BCCC

 also notes that the approval of that plan was not a contested case, as was in the CREZ

 case, to allow more robust vetting of the need determination at that time. BCCC agrees

 with the PFD and 4K Land & Cattle Company’s (“4K”) Exceptions to the PFD wherein

 the ALJ concluded that House Bill (“HB”) 5066 is a planning directive, not a construction

 mandate that removes the requirement for applicants to prove need in these projects.36

          Since then, demand has and is continuing to change. ERCOT appropriately

 adjusted its load-forecasting methodology to reduce the officer-letter attestation and data

 center loads in 2025.37 The Legislature also passed Senate Bill 6 in 2025 that required the

 Commission to adopt rules to reform the interconnection processes for large loads (over



          35 PFD at 53.

          36 PFD at 48-52; 4K at 5.


           PFD at Finding of Facts 87 and 133 at 90-91; Project 5599 Order Granting Good Cause
          37

Exception (June 5, 2025).


Burnet County Commissioners Court’s            10
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
  75 megawatts) to include financial contributions to interconnections costs, curtailment

 requirements for certain large loads through demand response programs and details about

 whether the large load will have on-site backup generating facilities as defined by the

 statute.38 This increased regulatory oversight places more economic risk on large loads

 interested in interconnecting to Texas. These changes may decrease large load interest in

 development in Texas.

         Furthermore, the Commission’s website reflects over 2000 megawatts of gas

generation will be in service in the Permian Basin by 2029.39 Competitive Power Ventures

has a planned gas generation facility of 1,350 megawatts in Ward County due to be online

in 2029.40 Vistra has a planned gas generation facility of 650 megawatts in Ward County

due to be online in 2028.41 The Commission is aware of these projects and should not

ignore them.

         Additional information relating to updated Permian Basin studies, letters from

Governor Abbott ordering the PUCT to revise cost allocation for data centers, as well as

Governor Abbott’s success with the Texas Energy Fund initiative42 and the changing mix

and volume of new load growth43 should be reconsidered before determining the issue of

need. Then, on August 3, 2026, Governor Abbott’s halt of data center approvals until the

Burnet County Commissioners Court’s               11
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
 PUCT and ERCOT complete an audit of the data centers wanting to connect to ERCOT

reflects the urgency of the proposed transmission lines may not be as high as Applicants

represent.44

         Until the multitude of issues found in the PFD that should have been proved by the

Applicants but were not, the Joint Application should be denied.45

    V.         CONCLUSION

         BCCC respectfully requests the Commission deny the Joint Application and adopt

the Proposal for Decision because:

         a. Joint Applicants’ failure to follow the Commission’s notice rules caused

               irreparable harm to the intervenors in this case in preparing their case and being

               heard;

         b. Joint Applicants’ failure to follow the Commission’s notice rules resulted in the

               information in the environmental assessment being inaccurate and stale;

         c. Legislation did not order the Commission plan to 2038;

         d. Legislation did not remove that the applicants were required to show need;

         e. Legislation did not require that the solutions to the Permian Basin be limited to

               transmission-only; and

         f. Circumstances have changed significantly and all of that information is known

               to the Commission.

         g. The Commission should not ignore new information creating new circumstance

               to the detriment of landowners in Texas.



         44
              https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-directs-comprehensive-data-center-audit
         45

Burnet County Commissioners Court’s                  12
Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision
         In the alternative, BCCC requests that the decision in this docket be delayed until

the deficiencies as stated above are corrected.

        In further alternative, if the Commission finds that the Joint Applicants carried their

burden in this proceeding, BCCC requests that ordering paragraphs be included as follows:

        1. Before completing engineering and design of any transmission towers or lines,

             Joint Applicants shall commission a study on the potential interference of

             765kV transmission lines and towers with Burnet County Commissioners

             Court’s emergency public safety communications systems, including potential

             Fresnel Zone Encroachment, gap discharge interference and corona discharge

             interference.

        2. Joint Applicants shall survey the location of Burnet County emergency

             communication towers in Burnet County to determine the actual locations of

             the emergency public safety communication towers.

        3. Joint Applicants shall consult with Burnet County Commissioners Court to

             mitigate any potential interference with Burnet County’s emergency public

             safety communications systems.
